```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.2, dpi = 144)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
out <- function(f) fread(file.path(params$output_dir, f))
info <- jsonlite::read_json(file.path(params$output_dir, "run_info.json"))
risk <- out("risk.csv")
supp <- out("suppressions.csv")
ind <- out("indicators.csv")
ovl <- out("ci_overlap.csv")
tab <- out("table_protected.csv")
tab_sum <- out("table_summary.csv")
checks <- out("release_checks.csv")
audit <- out("table_audit_income.csv")
audit0 <- out("table_audit_income_without_secondary.csv")

fmt <- function(x, d = 0) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

# Reference palette (validated categorical slots 1-3, neutral gray).
pal <- c(blue = "#2a78d6", orange = "#eb6834", aqua = "#1baf7a", gray = "#d9d8d4")
theme_report <- theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#ecebe8", linewidth = 0.3),
        axis.title = element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
        axis.text = element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
        plot.title.position = "plot",
        legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left")

orig <- risk[step == "no protection"]
final <- risk[step == "after local suppression"]
n_keys <- 8
scen_short <- function(x) sub(":.*", "", x)
```

<div class="alert alert-warning" role="note">
<strong>The data are synthetic.</strong> The EU-SILC public microdata are
simulated by Eurostat from models of the real survey: they contain no real
person, and Eurostat states that they cannot be used to draw conclusions about
the population. This project treats the file <em>as if</em> it were
confidential, to show the full disclosure-control workflow. All risk figures
and indicator values below illustrate the method; they say nothing about real
people or regions.
</div>

## Summary

This project plays the role of a statistical office that must release a
**public-use microdata file** and a **published table** from a household
survey without disclosing information about any respondent. It uses the
Italian file of the EU-SILC public microdata (`r info$year`,
`r fmt(info$persons)` persons aged 16 and over in `r fmt(info$households)`
households) as if it were the confidential source.

- In the original file, `r fmt(orig$sample_uniques)` records
  (`r pct(100 * orig$sample_uniques / orig$records)`) have a combination of
  eight publicly knowable characteristics that nobody else in the sample shares.
  The model-based estimate is `r fmt(orig$expected_reidentifications, 1)`
  expected re-identifications.
- Three protection scenarios were compared. All of them remove every sample
  unique. They differ in how much detail they sacrifice to get there.
- The recommended scenario, **`r final[scenario %like% "^S3", scenario]`**,
  leaves no combination shared by fewer than 5 records, also when the
  released weight is added to the keys, and reduces expected
  re-identifications to `r fmt(final[scenario %like% "^S3", expected_reidentifications], 2)`.
  It changes the income and poverty indicators by at most
  `r pct(ind[scenario %like% "^S3", max(abs(rel_diff_pct))], 2)`, almost all of
  it because the released weight can no longer differ between the NUTS 2
  regions of a NUTS 1 area.
- In the table of employee income by region, occupation and sex,
  `r tab_sum$primary` cells are sensitive and `r tab_sum$secondary` more
  are hidden so that no sensitive cell can be estimated too closely from the
  published cells. With the primary suppressions alone,
  `r sum(audit0$protected)` of the `r nrow(audit0)` sensitive cells are
  protected; with the secondary suppressions, `r sum(audit$protected)` of
  `r nrow(audit)` are.

## Why disclosure control

European statistics are produced under a legal duty of statistical
confidentiality (Regulation (EC) No 223/2009, Article 20, and Principle 5 of
the European Statistics Code of Practice). Removing names and identifiers is
not enough: a person can be recognised from a combination of ordinary
characteristics, such as region, age, household size and occupation.
Statistical disclosure control (SDC) measures that risk and reduces it while
keeping the data useful.

## Data and scenario

**Source.** Eurostat, EU-SILC public microdata for Italy, file
`IT_PUF_EUSILC.zip`, SHA-256 `r substr(info$sha256, 1, 16)`…, downloaded from
the Eurostat website. The public microdata are **fully synthetic**: they are
simulated from models of the real survey and contain no real respondent.
Eurostat states that they cannot be used for inference about the population.
Here they are used for what they are meant for: training and method
development. The risk figures below describe this synthetic file, not real
people.

**Intruder scenario.** An intruder knows some facts about a person and looks
for records that match them. The facts considered are the *key variables*
(quasi-identifiers):

| Key variable | EU-SILC variable | Detail in the source |
|---|---|---|
| Region | DB040 | NUTS 2 (21 regions) |
| Sex | PB150 | 2 categories |
| Age | PX020 | single years, 16 to 80+ |
| Marital status | PB190 | 5 categories |
| Citizenship | PB220A | Italy / other EU / non-EU |
| Education | PE040 | ISCED 1997, 7 levels |
| Occupation | PL051 | ISCO-08 major group, 9 groups |
| Household size | HX040 | 1 to 10 |

Survey identifiers (PB030, PX030) are direct identifiers and are replaced by
random numbers. Employee income (PY010G) and equivalised disposable income
(HY020 / HX050) are confidential numerical variables; household disposable
income and the equivalised household size are not released, because together
with equivalised income they would reveal household size. The personal weight
(PB040) is replaced by a released weight, described below, because the
original weight takes one value per NUTS 2 region and would reveal the region
in the scenarios that publish only NUTS 1.

## Risk in the original file

Two families of measures are used.

- **k-anonymity** counts records whose combination of keys appears fewer than
  *k* times in the sample. It needs no model and is easy to explain.
- **Individual risk** (Benedetti and Franconi, the method used by Istat and
  implemented in sdcMicro) estimates the probability that a match is correct,
  using the sampling weights to estimate how many people in the population
  share the same combination. The sum over records is the expected number of
  re-identifications. *Household risk* is the probability that at least one
  member of a household is re-identified, since identifying one member
  exposes the others.

```{r risk-original}
knitr::kable(
  data.table(
    Measure = c("Records", "Sample uniques", "Records violating 3-anonymity",
                "Records violating 5-anonymity", "Expected re-identifications",
                "Global risk", "Household risk"),
    Value = c(fmt(orig$records), fmt(orig$sample_uniques), fmt(orig$violating_3_anonymity),
              fmt(orig$violating_5_anonymity), fmt(orig$expected_reidentifications, 1),
              pct(orig$global_risk_pct, 2), pct(orig$household_risk_pct, 2))
  ), align = "lr")
```

The two families disagree, and the reason matters. About two thirds of the
records are unique in the sample, but each sampled person represents about 1,400
people (the mean weight), so the model expects few of those sample uniques to be
unique in the population as well. Agencies usually require both: a k-anonymity
threshold for the release file, and a check that the model-based risk is low.

## Protection methods

Each scenario applies three standard methods in this order (Hundepool et al.,
*Handbook on Statistical Disclosure Control*, 2012):

1. **Global recoding** of the key variables into broader categories.
2. **Local suppression**: individual key values are blanked, choosing the
   values that break the most risky combinations, until every combination is
   shared by at least *k* records. Region, sex and age are suppressed last
   because they matter most to users. Region and household size describe the
   household, and the release keeps a household identifier, so a value
   blanked for one member is blanked for every member of the household.
3. **Microaggregation** (MDAV, groups of 3) of the two income variables: each
   value is replaced by the mean of a group of three similar values, so no
   exact income is released. Equivalised income is treated once per
   household, so all members of a household keep the same value.

The released weight is the original weight post-stratified to the released
region: one value per released region (NUTS 2 in S1, NUTS 1 in S2 and S3)
and one national value for records whose region is blanked, so that regional
and national totals are unchanged. It carries no information below the
released region. The price is that, in S2 and S3, it no longer corrects for
the different sampling rates of the NUTS 2 regions inside a NUTS 1 area: any
weight that does so must differ between NUTS 2 regions, and so reveals them.

```{r scenarios}
knitr::kable(data.table(
  Scenario = c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
  Region = c("NUTS 2", "NUTS 1", "NUTS 1"),
  Age = c("5-year bands", "10-year bands", "10-year bands"),
  `Other keys` = c("source detail", "grouped", "grouped"),
  k = c(3, 3, 5)
), align = "lllll")
```

"Grouped" means: occupation in four skill groups, education as low / medium /
high, marital status as never married / married / previously married,
household size top-coded at 5 or more.

## Risk after protection

```{r risk-steps}
r <- risk[step != "no protection",
          .(Scenario = scen_short(scenario), Step = step,
            `Sample uniques` = fmt(sample_uniques),
            `< 3-anonymity` = fmt(violating_3_anonymity),
            `< 5-anonymity` = fmt(violating_5_anonymity),
            `Expected re-identifications` = fmt(expected_reidentifications, 2),
            `Household risk` = pct(household_risk_pct, 3))]
knitr::kable(r, align = "llrrrrr")
```

Recoding alone does most of the work for S2 and S3. In S1, which keeps
detailed codes, recoding leaves many combinations rare, so local suppression
has to blank many more values to reach the same guarantee.

### Release checks

Before a release file is written, four checks run on it; the pipeline stops
if one fails.

- **Smallest group with the weight as a key** (`min_fk_with_weight`): the
  smallest number of records sharing a combination of the eight keys *and*
  the released weight. It must be at least *k*.
- **Weights that point to one NUTS 2 region** (`weights_spanning_one_nuts2`):
  released weight values whose records all come from a single NUTS 2 region.
  It must be 0 in S2 and S3; it does not apply to S1, which publishes NUTS 2.
- **Households with inconsistent keys** (`households_inconsistent_keys`):
  households where region or household size is blank for some members and
  not for others. It must be 0.
- **Forbidden columns** (`forbidden_columns`): equivalised household size,
  household disposable income, survey identifiers or exact age in the
  release. It must be 0.

```{r release-checks}
ck <- copy(checks)[, `:=`(Scenario = scen_short(scenario),
                          value = ifelse(is.na(value), "n/a", fmt(value)),
                          pass = fcase(is.na(pass), "n/a", pass, "yes", default = "no"))]
ck <- dcast(ck, check ~ Scenario, value.var = c("value", "pass"))
ck <- ck[match(unique(checks$check), check)]
sc_ids <- intersect(c("S1", "S2", "S3"), unique(scen_short(checks$scenario)))
ck <- ck[, c("check", as.vector(rbind(paste0("value_", sc_ids), paste0("pass_", sc_ids)))), with = FALSE]
setnames(ck, c("Check", as.vector(rbind(paste(sc_ids, "value"), paste(sc_ids, "pass")))))
knitr::kable(ck, align = paste0("l", strrep("r", ncol(ck) - 1)))
fk_w <- checks[check == "min_fk_with_weight", setNames(value, scen_short(scenario))]
```

With the released weight added to the keys, the smallest group has
`r fmt(fk_w[["S1"]])` records in S1, `r fmt(fk_w[["S2"]])` in S2 and
`r fmt(fk_w[["S3"]])` in S3, so the claim that S3 leaves no combination shared
by fewer than 5 records holds for the weight too. Records with a blanked
region all share one national weight, which says only what the blank already
says, so in the group check their weight matches any value, like their
region, and in the NUTS 2 check that value is not counted (were their
weights different, they would be checked as they are).

## Information loss

### Suppressed values

```{r supp-chart, fig.height = 3.8}
s <- copy(supp)[, scenario := scen_short(scenario)]
labels <- c(region = "Region", sex = "Sex", age = "Age", marital = "Marital status",
            citizenship = "Citizenship", isced = "Education", isco1 = "Occupation",
            hh_size = "Household size")
s[, variable := factor(labels[variable], levels = rev(labels))]
ggplot(s, aes(x = suppressed, y = variable, fill = scenario)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.72) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(pal[c("blue", "orange", "aqua")]), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Values blanked by local suppression", y = NULL) +
  theme_report
```

```{r supp-table}
st <- supp[, .(`Values suppressed` = fmt(sum(suppressed)),
               `Share of key values` = pct(100 * sum(suppressed) / (orig$records * n_keys), 2)),
           by = .(Scenario = scen_short(scenario))]
knitr::kable(st, align = "lrr")
```

### Indicators

Each indicator is computed on the original and on the protected file with
the same code. The at-risk-of-poverty (AROP) rate is computed as in the
Eurostat indicator `ilc_li02` (threshold at 60% of the national median
equivalised disposable income), but on persons aged 16 and over with a
personal weight, because only the personal file is released. Because the
file is synthetic, the levels are not real Italian statistics; only the
differences matter.

The tables separate two sources of change. *Weight only* computes the
indicator on the original file with each record's weight replaced by its
released weight; *incomes only* replaces employee and equivalised income by
their microaggregated values; *released file* is the protected file as
published. The two partial effects do not add up exactly to the total,
because they interact and because records with a blanked region drop out of
the regional figures.

```{r indicator-sources}
mx <- ind[, .(w = max(abs(rel_diff_weight_pct)), i = max(abs(rel_diff_income_pct)),
              t = max(abs(rel_diff_pct))), by = .(sc = scen_short(scenario))]
mx <- setNames(split(mx, mx$sc), mx$sc)
top <- ind[scen_short(scenario) == "S3"][which.max(abs(rel_diff_weight_pct))]
nuts1_names <- c(ITC = "Nord-Ovest", ITF = "Sud", ITG = "Isole", ITH = "Nord-Est", ITI = "Centro")
top_domain <- if (top$domain %in% names(nuts1_names)) paste0(top$domain, ", ", nuts1_names[[top$domain]]) else top$domain
```

Microaggregation is the same in every scenario and moves no indicator by
more than `r pct(mx$S3$i, 2)`. In S1 the weight changes only through the
records with a blanked region, which get the national weight while the rest
of their region absorbs the difference; its effect is at most
`r pct(mx$S1$w, 2)`. In S2
and S3 the weight is the larger source: it is constant within each NUTS 1
area, so it no longer corrects for the different sampling rates of the NUTS 2
regions inside an area, and it moves indicators by up to
`r pct(mx$S3$w, 2)` (`r top$indicator`, `r top_domain`). That is the price
of not revealing NUTS 2 through the weight.

```{r indicators, results = "asis"}
for (sc in sort(unique(ind$scenario))) {
  iw <- ind[scenario == sc, .(Indicator = indicator, Domain = domain,
    `Original value` = ifelse(indicator %like% "AROP|Gini", fmt(value_original, 3), fmt(value_original)),
    `Weight only` = pct(rel_diff_weight_pct, 2),
    `Incomes only` = pct(rel_diff_income_pct, 2),
    `Released file` = pct(rel_diff_pct, 2))]
  cat(knitr::kable(iw, align = "llrrrr",
                   caption = paste0(sc, ". Relative difference from the original value")),
      sep = "\n")
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

### Regression

A user fitting a wage equation (log employee income on sex, age band and
NUTS 1 area, weighted) should reach the same conclusions on the protected
file. The confidence-interval overlap (Karr et al., 2006) is 1 when the 95%
intervals coincide and 0 when they do not overlap at all. The model is fitted
with `lm(weights = weight)`, which treats sampling weights as precision
weights, so its intervals are not design-based; they serve here only to
compare the two files. In S2 and S3 the overlap is lower for the same reason
as the indicators: the released weight changes the relative weight of the
NUTS 2 regions inside each NUTS 1 area, which shifts the regional and age
coefficients.

```{r overlap}
ov <- ovl[term != "(Intercept)", .(`Mean overlap` = round(mean(overlap), 2),
                                   `Lowest overlap` = round(min(overlap), 2),
                                   `Coefficients` = .N),
          by = .(Scenario = scen_short(scenario))]
knitr::kable(ov, align = "lrrr")
```

## Risk-utility trade-off

```{r ru-map, fig.height = 4}
ru <- rbind(
  data.table(label = "Original", loss = 0, er = orig$expected_reidentifications),
  merge(final[, .(scenario, er = expected_reidentifications)],
        supp[, .(loss = 100 * sum(suppressed) / (orig$records * n_keys)), by = scenario],
        by = "scenario")[, .(label = scen_short(scenario), loss, er)]
)
ggplot(ru, aes(x = loss, y = er)) +
  geom_point(size = 3.2, colour = pal[["blue"]]) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), nudge_x = 0.25, hjust = 0, size = 3.6, colour = "#0b0b0b") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.25))) +
  labs(x = "Key values suppressed (% of all key values)",
       y = "Expected re-identifications (log scale)") +
  theme_report
```

Points lower down are safer; points further left lose less detail. Global
recoding is not captured on the horizontal axis: S2 and S3 publish coarser
categories than S1 for every record.

**Recommendation.** S3 is the release candidate. It reaches 5-anonymity,
with the weight included, with far fewer suppressions than S1 because
recoding removed the rare categories first. Its cost is in the weight: S2
and S3 publish NUTS 1, so the weight cannot reflect NUTS 2, and indicators
move by up to `r pct(mx$S3$t, 2)` instead of `r pct(mx$S1$t, 2)` in S1.
Moving from S2 to S3 (k = 3 to k = 5) leaves the indicators as in S2,
roughly doubles the suppressions and removes the remaining records that share
their combination with only 3 or 4 others. S1 keeps regional detail but must
blank many more values, mostly occupation, and offers only 3-anonymity.
Users who need NUTS 2 detail should use the scientific-use file under a
research contract rather than a more detailed public file.

## Table protection

Published tables leak information too. The table is the estimated total
employee income by region (Italy, NUTS 1, NUTS 2), occupation (ISCO major
group) and sex: `r fmt(tab_sum$cells)` cells including all margins.

- **Primary suppression.** A cell is sensitive if it has fewer than 3
  contributors (threshold rule) or if the second-largest contributor could
  estimate the largest within 10% by subtracting its own value from the total
  (p% rule, p = 10).
- **Secondary suppression.** A suppressed cell could be recomputed from
  its row or column totals, so additional cells are hidden across the region
  hierarchy and both other dimensions. sdcTable's quick heuristic
  (`SIMPLEHEURISTIC`) is tried first, then its optimisation method (`OPT`);
  the first pattern that passes the audit below is published.
- **Audit.** For every sensitive cell, a linear program, independent of
  sdcTable, computes the lowest and highest income the cell can have given
  the published cells and the sums of the table. That interval must keep the
  true value at a distance of at least its p% protection level on both sides:
  the smallest error the second-largest contributor must be left with, so
  that it cannot estimate the largest contribution to within 10%.
- **Additions driven by the audit.** sdcTable's protection levels act on the
  number of contributors, not on income, so its pattern can leave an interval
  too narrow. When that happens, further cells are hidden around the failing
  cell, as rectangles or cubes of neighbouring cells (a sibling region, another
  occupation, the other sex), choosing the group that hides the least income
  and still protects the cell, and the audit is run again until every
  sensitive cell is protected.

```{r table-summary}
knitr::kable(data.table(
  Item = c("Cells", "Published", "Primary suppressions", "Secondary suppressions",
           "of which added by the audit",
           "Income in suppressed detailed cells",
           "Sensitive cells protected, primary suppressions only",
           "Sensitive cells protected, with secondary suppressions"),
  Value = c(fmt(tab_sum$cells), fmt(tab_sum$published), fmt(tab_sum$primary),
            fmt(tab_sum$secondary), fmt(tab_sum$cells_added),
            pct(tab_sum$income_hidden_pct, 1),
            paste(sum(audit0$protected), "of", nrow(audit0)),
            paste(sum(audit$protected), "of", nrow(audit)))
), align = "lr")
```

Secondary suppression method used: `r info$table_method`, with
`r info$table_cells_added` cells added by the audit. With the primary
suppressions alone, `r sum(audit0$protected)` of `r nrow(audit0)` sensitive
cells are protected; with the secondary suppressions,
`r sum(audit$protected)` of `r nrow(audit)` are. The published table and the
audit files give only which cells are suppressed and whether each sensitive
cell is protected; the values, contributions and intervals of the suppressed
cells are not published.

```{r table-pattern, fig.height = 6.2}
p <- tab[nchar(region) == 4 & occupation != "Total" & sex != "Total"]
p[, status := fcase(sdcStatus == "u", "Primary suppression",
                    sdcStatus == "x", "Secondary suppression",
                    default = "Published")]
p[, status := factor(status, levels = c("Published", "Primary suppression", "Secondary suppression"))]
p[, sex := fifelse(sex == "F", "Women", "Men")]
p[, occupation := sub("^OC0", "", occupation)]
p[occupation == "1", occupation := "0-1"]
p[, region := factor(region, levels = rev(sort(unique(region))))]
ggplot(p, aes(x = occupation, y = region, fill = status)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~sex) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`Published` = pal[["gray"]],
                               `Primary suppression` = pal[["orange"]],
                               `Secondary suppression` = pal[["blue"]]),
                    name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Occupation (ISCO-08 major group)", y = "NUTS 2 region") +
  theme_report + theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank())
```

```{r pattern-groups}
isco_names <- c(`0-1` = "managers", `2` = "professionals", `3` = "technicians",
                `4` = "clerical support workers", `5` = "service and sales workers",
                `6` = "skilled agricultural workers", `7` = "craft workers",
                `8` = "plant and machine operators", `9` = "elementary occupations")
groups_of <- function(who) {
  g <- p[status == "Primary suppression" & sex == who, .N, by = occupation][order(-N, occupation)]
  paste0(g$N, " for ", isco_names[g$occupation], " (group ", g$occupation, ")", collapse = ", ")
}
```

`r sum(p$status == "Primary suppression" & p$sex == "Women")` of the
`r sum(p$status == "Primary suppression")` sensitive detailed cells are for
women, in occupations with few female employees: `r groups_of("Women")`.
For men there are `r groups_of("Men")`. The secondary suppressions,
including the cells added by the audit, keep the interval of every
sensitive cell at least as wide as its p% protection level on both sides.

## Limitations

- The source is synthetic, so the risk levels are illustrative. On a real
  confidential file the same code would give different numbers.
- The intruder scenario fixes eight key variables. A different scenario (for
  example an intruder who knows income) needs its own key variables.
- Microaggregation by itself does not guarantee that a very high income
  cannot be linked to an outlier; a production release would add top-coding
  of income checked against the actual distribution.
- The released weight is constant within each released region. Real
  EU-SILC weights vary within regions by design; a production release would
  calibrate the weights to several published margins (for example sex and
  age band within NUTS 1) and run the same release checks on the result.
- The cells added after the audit are chosen one failing cell at a time; the
  final pattern is protected but not minimal. τ-ARGUS's modular method with
  income-based protection levels would usually hide less.

## Reproducibility

Source file pinned by SHA-256 in `data/manifest.json`; sdcMicro
`r info$sdcMicro`, sdcTable `r info$sdcTable`; run at `r info$run_at`.
Code: <https://github.com/simones99/eu-silc-sdc>.
